title: Ποδῶν νίψις
about: Penelope answers the stranger's promise that Odysseus will return within the year: she wishes it true but does not believe it, and she orders her attendants to bathe him and make up a bed, since a host's name is carried by the strangers he has treated well. The stranger refuses soft bedding; he has passed too many sleepless nights, and he will let only an old woman who has suffered as much as he has wash his feet. Penelope sends for Eurycleia, the nurse who raised Odysseus, who weeps for her lost master and remarks on how like him the stranger is. She prepares the cauldron, and Odysseus turns away from the firelight, afraid that she will touch the scar and learn who he is. She does, and at once recognises it. The poet then turns to tell how Odysseus got the scar: a boar's tusk on Parnassus, on a visit to his mother's father, Autolycus, who excelled all men in thievery and oaths through the gift of Hermes, and who was presented with the newborn Odysseus by Eurycleia herself.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is a reply-formula: τόν is the pronoun 'him' (in Homer the 'article' is a pronoun), αὖτε is 'again, in turn', and προσέειπε is the uncontracted aorist 'addressed' (Attic προσεῖπε). περίφρων is Penelope's standing epithet, 'circumspect' by the house rendering: it contains φρήν 'mind', 'thinking all round'. She is answering the stranger's oath, which closed the last part.

sentences.t: αἲ γὰρ τοῦτο, ξεῖνε, ἔπος τετελεσμένον εἴη·
sentences.l: “Would that this, stranger, word fulfilled might be;
sentences.i: “If only this word of yours, stranger, might be fulfilled;
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ opens a wish, 'would that'. ἔπος is 'word', here the stranger's promise that Odysseus will come; τετελεσμένον is the perfect passive participle of τελέω 'fulfil', and with εἴη (optative of εἰμί) it makes a wish about something finished: 'might be fulfilled'. ξεῖνε is 'stranger', the courteous form for a guest. The speech is Penelope's.

sentences.t:
τῷ κε τάχα γνοίης φιλότητά τε πολλά τε δῶρα
ἐξ ἐμεῦ, ὡς ἄν τίς σε συναντόμενος μακαρίζοι.
sentences.l:
then soon you would know friendship and many gifts
from me, so that someone meeting you would call you blessed.”
sentences.i: Then you would soon know friendship from me, and many gifts, so that anyone who met you would call you blessed.”
sentences.n: τῷ is 'then, in that case'; κε with the optative γνοίης (from γιγνώσκω) gives 'you would know', the result of the wish just made. φιλότητα is 'friendship' and δῶρα 'gifts'. ἐξ ἐμεῦ is 'from me' (ἐμεῦ is the Ionic genitive of ἐγώ). ὡς ἄν with the optative μακαρίζοι is 'so that … would call blessed'; συναντόμενος is 'meeting'. Her speech does not end here but turns to doubt in the next line.

sentences.t: ἀλλά μοι ὧδ’ ἀνὰ θυμὸν ὀΐεται, ὡς ἔσεταί περ·
sentences.l: But to me thus in my heart it seems, as indeed it will be;
sentences.i: But in my heart it seems to me that this is how it will be, and so it will;
sentences.n: ἀλλά μοι ὧδ’ ἀνὰ θυμὸν ὀΐεται: the verb ὀΐεται (ὀΐομαι 'suppose, foresee') is used of what seems so to someone, with μοι 'to me' and ὧδε 'thus'; what seems so follows in the next lines. ἀνὰ θυμόν is 'in my heart'. ὡς ἔσεταί περ is 'just as it will be': ἔσεται is the epic future of εἰμί and περ 'indeed' stresses it.

sentences.t:
οὔτ’ Ὀδυσεὺς ἔτι οἶκον ἐλεύσεται, οὔτε σὺ πομπῆς
τεύξῃ, ἐπεὶ οὐ τοῖοι σημάντορές εἰσ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
οἷος Ὀδυσσεὺς ἔσκε μετ’ ἀνδράσιν, εἴ ποτ’ ἔην γε,
ξείνους αἰδοίους ἀποπεμπέμεν ἠδὲ δέχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
Neither Odysseus any more to his house will come, nor you of an escort
will get, since not such overseers are in the house
as Odysseus was among men, if ever he was,
revered strangers to send off and to receive.
sentences.i: Odysseus will never come to his house again, and you will get no escort, since there are no such overseers in the house as Odysseus was among men, if ever he was, to send revered strangers on their way and to receive them.
sentences.n: οὔτ’ … οὔτε is 'neither … nor'; ἐλεύσεται is the future of ἔρχομαι. πομπῆς τεύξῃ is 'you will get an escort': τεύξῃ is the future middle of τυγχάνω (τεύξεαι contracted), 'you will get', and τυγχάνω takes the genitive. τοῖοι … οἷος is 'such … as'. σημάντορες is 'overseers', those who give directions (σημαίνω 'signal'). ἔσκε is the iterative 'used to be' (the -σκ- ending), and ἔην is the epic imperfect of εἰμί (= Attic ἦν), so εἴ ποτ’ ἔην γε is 'if ever he was'. ξείνους αἰδοίους is 'revered strangers' (αἰδοῖος 'revered', owed αἰδώς). ἀποπεμπέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν (= ἀποπέμπειν).

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μιν, ἀμφίπολοι, ἀπονίψατε, κάτθετε δ’ εὐνήν,
δέμνια καὶ χλαίνας καὶ ῥήγεα σιγαλόεντα,
ὥς κ’ εὖ θαλπιόων χρυσόθρονον Ἠῶ ἵκηται.
sentences.l:
But him, attendants, wash off, and lay down a couch,
bedding and cloaks and glossy rugs,
so that, well warmed, golden-throned Dawn he may reach.
sentences.i: Attendants, wash him, and make up a couch for him, with bedding, cloaks and glossy rugs, so that he may keep warm and reach golden-throned Dawn in comfort.
sentences.n: ἀπονίψατε is the aorist imperative of ἀπονίζω 'wash off', and κάτθετε is the aorist imperative of κατατίθημι 'put down, lay out', with κατά shortened to κατ- before θετε; εὐνήν is 'couch'. ἀμφίπολοι is 'attendants', the vocative. μιν is 'him', the stranger. δέμνια is 'bedding'; ῥήγεα are 'rugs', and σιγαλόεντα 'glossy' by the house rendering. θαλπιόων is the participle of θαλπιάω 'be warm' (from θάλπω), stretched by diectasis. ὥς κ(ε) with the subjunctive ἵκηται is purpose, 'so that he may reach'. χρυσόθρονον is 'golden-throned': θρόνος is 'chair', though an old alternative takes the second part to be θρόνα 'embroidered flowers'.

sentences.t:
ἠῶθεν δὲ μάλ’ ἦρι λοέσσαι τε χρῖσαί τε,
ὥς κ’ ἔνδον παρὰ Τηλεμάχῳ δείπνοιο μέδηται
ἥμενος ἐν μεγάρῳ·
sentences.i: And at dawn, very early, bathe him and anoint him, so that he may sit inside the hall beside Telemachus and turn his thoughts to his meal;
sentences.n: ἠῶθεν is 'from dawn, at dawn' (the suffix -θεν), and ἦρι is 'early'. λοέσσαι and χρῖσαι are infinitives with the force of orders, continuing the imperative of line 317: 'bathe, anoint'. ὥς κ(ε) … μέδηται is purpose again; μέδομαι 'take thought of, turn one's mind to' takes the genitive δείπνοιο ('of the meal'; -οιο = -ου). ἥμενος is 'sitting' (ἧμαι), and μεγάρῳ is the 'hall'. Telemachus is Τηλεμάχῳ, dative after παρά.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄλγιον ὅς κεν ἐκείνων
τοῦτον ἀνιάζῃ θυμοφθόρος·
sentences.l:
and the more painful for whichever of them
vexes this man, heart-destroying;
sentences.i: and so much the more painful for any of them who torments him, heart-destroying as he is;
sentences.n: τῷ δ’ ἄλγιον is 'and the more painful (for him)': ἄλγιον is the comparative of ἀλγεινός. ἐκείνων is 'of those', the suitors, who are not named. ὅς κεν with the subjunctive ἀνιάζῃ is 'whoever may vex'. θυμοφθόρος is built from θυμός 'heart' and φθείρω 'destroy'; the word does not make plain whether the heart destroyed is the vexer's or his victim's, and the English keeps the compound.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι ἔργον
ἐνθάδ’ ἔτι πρήξει, μάλα περ κεχολωμένος αἰνῶς.
sentences.l:
and not any deed
here any more will he accomplish, though very much enraged, fearsomely.
sentences.i: and no matter how terribly angry he is, he will accomplish nothing more here.
sentences.n: οὐδέ τι ἔργον … πρήξει is 'he will do no deed at all'; πρήξει is the Ionic spelling of πράξει. ἔτι is 'any longer'. μάλα περ κεχολωμένος is 'however much enraged': περ makes the participle concessive, and κεχολωμένος is the perfect passive participle of χολόω 'anger'. αἰνῶς, from αἰνός 'fearsome', is the adverb 'terribly'.

sentences.t:
πῶς γὰρ ἐμεῦ σύ, ξεῖνε, δαήσεαι εἴ τι γυναικῶν
ἀλλάων περίειμι νόον καὶ ἐπίφρονα μῆτιν,
εἴ κεν ἀϋσταλέος, κακὰ εἱμένος ἐν μεγάροισιν
δαινύῃ;
sentences.l:
For how of me will you, stranger, find out if at all of women
others I surpass in mind and in thoughtful cunning,
if unkempt, badly clothed, in my halls
you were to feast?
sentences.i: How, stranger, will you find out whether I surpass other women in mind and thoughtful cunning, if you dine in my halls squalid and in poor clothes?
sentences.n: πῶς γάρ … 'for how …' gives her reason; δαήσεαι is the future of δάω 'learn, find out'. εἴ τι is 'whether at all'. περίειμι is 'I surpass' and takes the genitive γυναικῶν ἀλλάων (ἀλλάων = ἄλλων, 'other'). νόον is 'mind' and ἐπίφρονα μῆτιν 'thoughtful cunning': μῆτις is 'cunning intelligence' and ἐπίφρων 'thoughtful'. ἀϋσταλέος is traditionally 'squalid, unwashed', but its exact sense is not certain. κακὰ εἱμένος is 'clad in poor things' (perfect passive participle of ἕννυμι). εἴ κεν δαινύῃ is a subjunctive condition: 'if you should feast'.

sentences.t: ἄνθρωποι δὲ μινυνθάδιοι τελέθουσιν.
sentences.l: and men are short-lived.
sentences.i: For men are short-lived.
sentences.n: μινυνθάδιοι is 'short-lived, lasting but a little while'. τελέθουσιν is the plural of τελέθω 'be, come to be', which Homer uses in place of εἰσί. The δέ is only a loose 'and'; the sense it adds is explanatory, which the 'For' of the i layer brings out: men are short-lived, so what outlasts a man is his name.

sentences.t:
ὃς μὲν ἀπηνὴς αὐτὸς ἔῃ καὶ ἀπηνέα εἰδῇ,
τῷ δὲ καταρῶνται πάντες βροτοὶ ἄλγε’ ὀπίσσω
ζωῷ, ἀτὰρ τεθνεῶτί γ’ ἐφεψιόωνται ἅπαντες·
sentences.i: Whoever is unkind himself and knows only unkindness, all mortals call down pains upon him in the time to come while he lives, and when he is dead they all mock him;
sentences.n: ὃς μέν … τῷ δέ …: ὅς with the subjunctives ἔῃ (= ᾖ, 'be') and εἰδῇ (from οἶδα) is 'whoever is … and knows'; τῷ is the resumptive 'him'. ἀπηνής is 'unkind' by the house rendering ('unfriendly, harsh' in the lexica), and ἀπηνέα εἰδῇ is 'knows unkind things'. καταρῶνται is 'call down curses' (καταράομαι). ἄλγε’ is ἄλγεα, and ὀπίσσω 'hereafter'. ζωῷ … τεθνεῶτι are datives, 'to him living … to him dead'. ἐφεψιόωνται is 'mock' (ἐφεψιάομαι, stretched by diectasis); the same verb returns in 370, and in 372 with κατά (καθεψιόωνται).

sentences.t:
ὃς δ’ ἂν ἀμύμων αὐτὸς ἔῃ καὶ ἀμύμονα εἰδῇ,
τοῦ μέν τε κλέος εὐρὺ δὶα ξεῖνοι φορέουσι
πάντας ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπους, πολλοί τέ μιν ἐσθλὸν ἔειπον.
sentences.l:
but whoever blameless himself is and knows blameless things,
of him the wide fame strangers carry throughout
to all men, and many call him good.”
sentences.i: But whoever is blameless himself and knows blameless things, his wide fame is carried by strangers far and wide to all men, and many call him good.”
sentences.n: ὃς δ’ ἂν … answers ὃς μέν above. ἀμύμων is 'blameless' by the house rendering, though the real meaning of ἀμύμων is not known. κλέος εὐρύ is 'wide fame'; μέν τε carries the epic τε of a general truth. δὶα is διά, 'through', and with φορέουσι 'they carry' it gives 'carry far and wide'; ξεῖνοι 'strangers' are the travellers who spread a host's name, which is why his treatment of guests matters. ἔειπον is the aorist of 'say', here 'call', in a general statement. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη is the reply-formula 'answering her he addressed': τήν is the pronoun 'her', ἀπαμειβόμενος 'answering', προσέφη 'addressed'. πολύμητις is 'many-wiled, of many wiles'; μῆτις is 'cunning intelligence'. Odysseus replies to Penelope's speech, and his reply turns first on the bed she has ordered made up.

sentences.t:
ὦ γύναι αἰδοίη Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος,
ἦ τοι ἐμοὶ χλαῖναι καὶ ῥήγεα σιγαλόεντα
ἤχθεθ’, ὅτε πρῶτον Κρήτης ὄρεα νιφόεντα
νοσφισάμην ἐπὶ νηὸς ἰὼν δολιχηρέτμοιο,
sentences.l:
“O wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes, revered one,
truly to me cloaks and glossy rugs
were hateful, when first the snowy mountains of Crete
I left behind, going on a long-oared ship,
sentences.i: “Revered wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes, cloaks and glossy rugs became hateful to me from the time I first left the snowy mountains of Crete behind, sailing in a long-oared ship,
sentences.n: γύναι is 'wife' (literally 'woman'), here with the genitive of her husband's name; αἰδοίη is 'revered'. Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος is 'Odysseus, son of Laertes' (-άδεω is the epic genitive; Ὀδυσῆος and Ὀδυσσῆος are the same name, spelled to fit the verse). ἦ τοι is 'truly'. ἤχθεθ’ is a form of the verb behind ἐχθρός 'hateful': 'became hateful to me'. ὅτε πρῶτον is 'when first'; νοσφισάμην is 'I left behind, turned away from', with the accusative ὄρεα 'mountains'; νιφόεντα is 'snowy'. δολιχηρέτμοιο is 'long-oared' (δολιχός 'long', ἐρετμόν 'oar'), and ἐπὶ νηὸς ἰών is 'going on a ship'.

sentences.t: κείω δ’ ὡς τὸ πάρος περ ἀΰπνους νύκτας ἴαυον·
sentences.l: and I will lie as indeed formerly sleepless nights I passed;
sentences.i: and I shall lie as I did before, when I passed sleepless nights;
sentences.n: κείω is a first-person form of κεῖμαι 'lie' with the sense 'I will lie'; the exact class of the form is disputed. ὡς τὸ πάρος περ is 'just as before'. ἀΰπνους is 'sleepless' (ἀ- + ὕπνος), and ἴαυον is the imperfect of ἰαύω 'pass the night, lie'. He refuses the soft bed by saying that he is used to bad nights.

sentences.t:
πολλὰς γὰρ δὴ νύκτας ἀεικελίῳ ἐνὶ κοίτῃ
ἄεσα καί τ’ ἀνέμεινα ἐΰθρονον Ἠῶ δῖαν.
sentences.l:
For many nights indeed on an unseemly resting-place
I spent, and waited for fair-throned Dawn, heavenly.
sentences.i: I spent many nights on an unseemly resting-place, and waited for fair-throned, heavenly Dawn.
sentences.n: πολλὰς … νύκτας is an accusative of duration, 'for many nights'. ἀεικελίῳ is ἀεικέλιος 'unseemly', and κοίτῃ 'resting-place' (κοίτη 'bed, lair'). ἄεσα is the aorist of ἄω 'spend the night' (also 'sleep'); ἀνέμεινα is 'I waited for' (ἀναμένω). ἐΰθρονον is 'fair-throned' (ἐΰ- 'fair'), and Ἠῶ is the accusative of Ἠώς; δῖαν is 'heavenly' by the house rendering.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί μοι ποδάνιπτρα ποδῶν ἐπιήρανα θυμῷ
γίγνεται·
sentences.l:
Nor in any way to me foot-baths of the feet welcome in my heart
do they become;
sentences.i: nor are foot-baths in any way welcome to my heart;
sentences.n: ποδάνιπτρα are 'foot-baths', the water or basin for washing feet; ποδῶν 'of the feet' repeats what the compound already says, and τί is adverbial, 'in any way'. ἐπιήρανα is an unusual form of an adjective meaning 'welcome, pleasing', and θυμῷ is 'in my heart', a dative of interest. γίγνεται is singular with the neuter plural subject, as in Attic: 'becomes, proves'.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γυνὴ ποδὸς ἅψεται ἡμετέροιο
τάων αἵ τοι δῶμα κάτα δρήστειραι ἔασιν,
εἰ μή τις γρηῦς ἔστι παλαιή, κεδνὰ ἰδυῖα,
ἥ τις δὴ τέτληκε τόσα φρεσὶν ὅσσα τ’ ἐγώ περ·
sentences.l:
nor will any woman touch my foot
of those who for you throughout the house are the serving-women,
unless there is some old woman, aged, the one wise and trusty,
who has indeed endured in her mind as much as I.
sentences.i: No woman among those who do your work throughout the house will touch my foot, unless there is some old woman, aged and trusty and wise, who has endured as much in her mind as I have.
sentences.n: ἅψεται is the future of ἅπτομαι 'touch', which takes the genitive ποδός; ἡμετέροιο is 'our' used for 'my' (-οιο = -ου). τάων is the demonstrative 'of those' (the relative is αἵ), and τοι is 'for you' or 'I tell you'; δῶμα κάτα is 'throughout the house' (κατά placed after its noun). δρήστειραι is 'serving-women', and ἔασιν is εἰσίν. γρηῦς is 'old woman' (Attic γραῦς). κεδνὰ ἰδυῖα is 'trusty and wise': κεδνά is 'careful, trusty', and ἰδυῖα is the feminine participle of οἶδα 'knowing'. τέτληκε is the perfect of τλάω 'endure', and τόσα … ὅσσα τ’ ἐγώ περ is 'as much as I'.

sentences.t: τῇ δ’ οὐκ ἂν φθονέοιμι ποδῶν ἅψασθαι ἐμεῖο.
sentences.l: To her I would not begrudge to touch my feet.”
sentences.i: I would not begrudge her touching my feet.”
sentences.n: τῇ is 'to her'. φθονέοιμι is the optative of φθονέω 'begrudge', and with ἄν it is a polite 'I would not'. ποδῶν ἅψασθαι is 'to touch the feet', the same construction as in 344, and ἐμεῖο is the epic genitive of ἐγώ. The speech ends: he will accept only an old woman.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The same reply-formula as line 308, now opening Penelope's second speech: τὸν … αὖτε προσέειπε 'addressed him in turn', with her standing epithet περίφρων 'circumspect'.

sentences.t: ξεῖνε φίλ’·
sentences.l: “Dear stranger;
sentences.i: “Dear stranger,
sentences.n: ξεῖνε φίλ’ is ξεῖνε φίλε with the final vowel elided: 'dear stranger', the house rendering of the friendly address. The Greek marks a stop after it with the ano teleia, and the reason follows in the next unit.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πώ τις ἀνὴρ πεπνυμένος ὧδε
ξείνων τηλεδαπῶν φιλίων ἐμὸν ἵκετο δῶμα,
ὡς σὺ μάλ’ εὐφραδέως πεπνυμένα πάντ’ ἀγορεύεις·
sentences.i: For no man so prudent among friendly strangers from far-off lands has ever yet come to my house as you, saying every prudent thing so eloquently;
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ πώ τις … is 'for not yet any'. πεπνυμένος is 'prudent' by the house rendering, and πεπνυμένα in 352 is the same word on 'things': a deliberate echo. ξείνων τηλεδαπῶν φιλίων is a partitive genitive, 'among strangers from far lands, friendly ones': τηλεδαπός is 'from a far-off land' and φίλιος 'friendly'. ἵκετο is the unaugmented 'came'. εὐφραδέως is 'eloquently' (εὖ + the stem of φράζω 'tell'), and ἀγορεύεις 'you say'.

sentences.t:
ἔστι δέ μοι γρηῢς πυκινὰ φρεσὶ μήδε’ ἔχουσα
ἣ κεῖνον δύστηνον ἐῢ τρέφεν ἠδ’ ἀτίταλλε,
δεξαμένη χείρεσσ’, ὅτε μιν πρῶτον τέκε μήτηρ,
ἥ σε πόδας νίψει, ὀλιγηπελέουσά περ ἔμπης.
sentences.l:
But there is for me an old woman, solid counsels in her mind having,
who that wretched man well reared and fostered,
receiving him in her hands, when first his mother bore him;
she will wash your feet, faint with little strength though she is, all the same.
sentences.i: I have an old woman whose mind holds solid counsels, who reared that wretched man well and fostered him, taking him in her hands when his mother first bore him; she will wash your feet, faint though she is, all the same.
sentences.n: ἔστι δέ μοι is 'and there is for me', 'I have'. γρηῢς is the same word as γρηῦς in 346, the Ionic form of Attic γραῦς 'old woman'. πυκινά is 'solid' by the house rendering (as in the 'solid house'), and μήδεα is 'counsels'. κεῖνον is 'that man', Odysseus, who is not named; δύστηνον is 'wretched'. τρέφεν and ἀτίταλλε are unaugmented imperfects, 'reared' and 'fostered' (ἀτιτάλλω 'bring up a child'). δεξαμένη is 'receiving' (δέχομαι), the old woman taking the newborn in her hands, and τέκε is 'bore'. νίψει is the future of νίζω 'wash'. ὀλιγηπελέουσα is 'faint', literally 'with little strength'; περ ἔμπης is 'though … all the same'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ἀνστᾶσα, περίφρων Εὐρύκλεια,
νίψον σοῖο ἄνακτος ὁμήλικα·
sentences.l:
But come now, rising up, circumspect Eurycleia,
wash a man of an age with your lord;
sentences.i: But come now, get up, circumspect Eurycleia, and wash a man of an age with your lord;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν is 'but come now'. ἀνστᾶσα is the aorist participle of ἀνίστημι 'standing up'. περίφρων Εὐρύκλεια gives Eurycleia the epithet that Penelope bears in the formula of 308: 'circumspect'. νίψον is the aorist imperative of νίζω. σοῖο ἄνακτος is 'of your lord' (σοῖο is the epic genitive of the possessive σός, agreeing with ἄνακτος; ἄναξ 'lord'), the master of the house, Odysseus. ὁμήλικα is 'of the same age'. The Greek does not say 'the stranger' but leaves him to be understood.

sentences.t:
καί που Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἤδη τοιόσδ’ ἐστὶ πόδας τοιόσδε τε χεῖρας·
sentences.l:
and perhaps Odysseus
by now is such as this man in feet, and such in hands;
sentences.i: perhaps Odysseus too is by now just like him in his feet and hands;
sentences.n: καί που is 'and perhaps'. τοιόσδε is 'such as this one here', pointing at the stranger; πόδας and χεῖρας are accusatives of respect, 'in feet, in hands'. ἤδη is 'by now'. The comparison joins the stranger and the absent husband in a single bodily likeness, which Eurycleia takes up.

sentences.t: αἶψα γὰρ ἐν κακότητι βροτοὶ καταγηράσκουσιν.
sentences.l: for quickly in misery mortals grow old.”
sentences.i: for mortals age quickly in misery.”
sentences.n: αἶψα is 'quickly'. κακότητι is the dative of κακότης 'misery, wretchedness'. καταγηράσκουσιν is 'grow old' (καταγηράσκω), and βροτοί 'mortals'. It is a general statement in the present tense, and it closes Penelope's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, γρηῢς δὲ κατέσχετο χερσὶ πρόσωπα,
δάκρυα δ’ ἔκβαλε θερμά, ἔπος δ’ ὀλοφυδνὸν ἔειπεν·
sentences.l:
So then she spoke, and the old woman covered with her hands her face,
tears she cast out, hot, and a word of lament she spoke:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and the old woman covered her face with her hands and wept hot tears, and spoke a word of lament:
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη is 'so then she spoke'. γρηῢς is 'the old woman', Eurycleia, who has just been named. κατέσχετο is the aorist middle of κατέχω 'hold, cover', with χερσί 'with her hands' and πρόσωπα 'face' (Homer often uses the plural). ἔκβαλε is 'cast out', unaugmented. ὀλοφυδνόν is 'mournful, of lament' (from ὀλοφύρομαι). ἔειπεν is the aorist of 'say'. Her words follow.

sentences.t: ὤ μοι ἐγὼ σέο, τέκνον, ἀμήχανος·
sentences.l: “Oh me, I, on your account, child, helpless;
sentences.i: “Oh me, child, I am helpless for your sake;
sentences.n: ὤ μοι ἐγώ is a cry of distress, 'oh me, I'. σέο is the epic genitive of σύ, 'on your account'. τέκνον is 'child', how an old nurse addresses the man she raised. ἀμήχανος is 'helpless', literally 'without resource' (ἀ- + μηχανή 'device'), a nominative describing the speaker; the Greek has no verb.

sentences.t:
ἦ σε περὶ Ζεὺς
ἀνθρώπων ἤχθηρε θεουδέα θυμὸν ἔχοντα.
sentences.l:
Truly you exceeding Zeus
than men hated, a god-fearing heart having.
sentences.i: Truly Zeus hated you beyond all men, though your heart was god-fearing.
sentences.n: ἦ is 'truly'. περί is an adverb here, 'exceedingly', and ἀνθρώπων is a genitive of comparison, 'more than men'. ἤχθηρε is the aorist of ἐχθαίρω 'hate'. θεουδέα is 'god-fearing', the accusative of θεουδής (usually explained from θεός and δέος 'fear'); it agrees with θυμόν 'heart', and ἔχοντα agrees with σε: 'you, having a god-fearing heart'.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πώ τις τόσσα βροτῶν Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ
πίονα μηρί’ ἔκη’ οὐδ’ ἐξαίτους ἑκατόμβας,
ὅσσα σὺ τῷ ἐδίδους, ἀρώμενος ἧος ἵκοιο
γῆράς τε λιπαρὸν θρέψαιό τε φαίδιμον υἱόν·
sentences.l:
For not yet any of mortals to bolt-delighting Zeus
fat thigh-pieces burned, nor picked-out hecatombs,
as many as you to him used to give, praying until you should reach
a sleek old age and rear a glorious son;
sentences.i: For no mortal has ever burned so many fat thigh-pieces or choice hecatombs to Zeus, who delights in the thunderbolt, as you used to give him, praying that you might reach a sleek old age and rear a glorious son;
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ πώ τις … is 'for not yet any'; τόσσα … ὅσσα is 'so many … as'. Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ is 'bolt-delighting Zeus' (τέρπω 'delight' + κεραυνός 'thunderbolt'), in the house rendering. μηρία are the 'thigh-pieces' burned for the gods, and ἔκη’ is the aorist of καίω 'burn'. ἐξαίτους is 'picked out, choice', and ἑκατόμβας 'hecatombs', large sacrifices (the word holds ἑκατόν 'hundred'). ἐδίδους is 'you used to give'. ἀρώμενος is 'praying', and ἧος is properly 'until', here introducing what the prayer asked, with the optatives ἵκοιο 'you might reach' and θρέψαιο 'you might rear'. λιπαρόν is 'sleek, shining'; φαίδιμος is 'glorious' by the house rendering.

sentences.t: νῦν δέ τοι οἴῳ πάμπαν ἀφείλετο νόστιμον ἦμαρ.
sentences.l: But now to you alone altogether he took away the homecoming day.
sentences.i: But now he has taken from you alone the day of your homecoming.
sentences.n: νῦν δέ is 'but now', the turn from the sacrifices to what came of them. τοι is 'to you' and οἴῳ 'alone' (οἶος). πάμπαν is 'altogether'. ἀφείλετο is the aorist middle of ἀφαιρέομαι 'take away from', and its subject is still Zeus. νόστιμον ἦμαρ is 'the homecoming day', the day that would bring one home (νόστος).

sentences.t:
οὕτω που καὶ κείνῳ ἐφεψιόωντο γυναῖκες
ξείνων τηλεδαπῶν, ὅτε τευ κλυτὰ δώμαθ’ ἵκοιτο,
sentences.l:
So, I suppose, at him also were mocking the women
of strangers from far-off lands, whenever to anyone’s famous halls he came,
sentences.i: So too, I suppose, the women of strangers from far-off lands mocked him whenever he came to anyone’s famous halls,
sentences.n: οὕτω που is 'so, I suppose'. κείνῳ is 'at him', Odysseus, a dative with ἐφεψιόωντο 'mocked' (the verb of 331). The ξεῖνοι here are the hosts he visited, 'strangers' from where he stood, and their women are those of the households he came to. τευ is the epic τινός, 'anyone's'. ὅτε … ἵκοιτο is an optative of repeated occasion, 'whenever he came'. δώμαθ’ is δώματα, and κλυτά is 'famous'.

sentences.t:
ὡς σέθεν αἱ κύνες αἵδε καθεψιόωνται ἅπασαι,
τάων νῦν λώβην τε καὶ αἴσχεα πόλλ’ ἀλεείνων
οὐκ ἐάᾳς νίζειν·
sentences.i: just as all these dogs here mock you, and it is to avoid their outrage and their many shames that you now will not let them wash you;
sentences.n: ὡς … answers οὕτω in 370: 'just as … so'. σέθεν is the epic genitive of σύ, 'at you', with καθεψιόωνται 'mock', the same verb as ἐφεψιόωντο. αἱ κύνες αἵδε is 'these dogs here': κύων 'dog' is a term of abuse for a shameless woman, and the feminine article shows that she means the women servants of the house. τάων is 'of whom'; λώβη is 'outrage, insult', αἴσχεα 'shames', and ἀλεείνων 'avoiding'. οὐκ ἐάᾳς is οὐκ ἐᾷς 'you do not allow', with the vowels stretched back out by diectasis, and νίζειν 'to wash (you)'.

sentences.t:
ἐμὲ δ’ οὐκ ἀέκουσαν ἄνωγε
κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο, περίφρων Πηνελόπεια.
sentences.l:
but me, not unwilling, bids
the daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope.
sentences.i: but the daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope, has bidden me, and I am not unwilling.
sentences.n: ἐμὲ δ’ οὐκ ἀέκουσαν ἄνωγε: ἀέκουσαν is 'unwilling' (ἀέκων), and the negative makes the understatement 'not unwilling', that is, glad. ἄνωγε is a perfect with present sense, 'she bids'. κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο is 'the daughter of Icarius' (-οιο = -ου), the subject, named at the end of the clause with περίφρων Πηνελόπεια 'circumspect Penelope'.

sentences.t:
τῷ σε πόδας νίψω ἅμα τ’ αὐτῆς Πηνελοπείης
καὶ σέθεν εἵνεκ’, ἐπεί μοι ὀρώρεται ἔνδοθι θυμὸς
κήδεσιν.
sentences.l:
Therefore your feet I will wash, both for Penelope herself
and for your sake, since for me is stirred within the heart
with sorrows.
sentences.i: That is why I shall wash your feet, both for Penelope herself and for your sake, since my heart is stirred within me with sorrows.
sentences.n: τῷ is 'therefore'; νίψω is the future of νίζω. ἅμα τ’ … καὶ … is 'both … and', joining 'for Penelope herself' and 'for you', and εἵνεκ’ (ἕνεκα) governs both genitives, αὐτῆς Πηνελοπείης and σέθεν (the epic genitive of σύ). ὀρώρεται is the perfect middle of ὄρνυμι 'rouse', 'is stirred up'; ἔνδοθι is 'within'. κήδεσιν is 'with sorrows' (κῆδος 'care, sorrow'), a dative of cause.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ξυνίει ἔπος, ὅττι κεν εἴπω·
sentences.l: But come now, attend to the word, whatever I may say;
sentences.i: But come now, attend to what I say:
sentences.n: ξυνίει is the imperative of συνίημι 'take in, understand' (ξυν- is the epic spelling of συν-). ὅττι κεν εἴπω is an indefinite relative clause with κεν and the aorist subjunctive, 'whatever I may say'. What she wants understood follows.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ δὴ ξεῖνοι ταλαπείριοι ἐνθάδ’ ἵκοντο,
ἀλλ’ οὔ πώ τινά φημι ἐοικότα ὧδε ἰδέσθαι
ὡς σὺ δέμας φωνήν τε πόδας τ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ ἔοικας.
sentences.l:
Many, indeed, strangers much-tried here have come,
but not yet anyone, I say, so like to look at
as you in body and voice and feet to Odysseus are like.”
sentences.i: Many much tried strangers have come here, but I tell you I have never yet seen anyone look as much like Odysseus as you do, in body, voice and feet.”
sentences.n: πολλοὶ δή is 'many indeed'. ταλαπείριοι is 'much-tried' (πεῖρα 'trial'), and ἵκοντο is the unaugmented 'came'. φημί is 'I say'. οὔ πώ τινα … ἐοικότα is 'not yet anyone resembling', and ἰδέσθαι is an infinitive of respect, 'to look at'. ὧδε … ὡς is 'so … as'. δέμας, φωνήν and πόδας are accusatives of respect, 'in body, in voice, in feet', and ἔοικας is 'you resemble', with the dative Ὀδυσῆϊ. This closes her speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: The same reply-formula as line 335, now introducing Odysseus's answer to Eurycleia: τὴν … ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη 'answering her he addressed', with πολύμητις 'of many wiles'.

sentences.t:
ὦ γρηῦ, οὕτω φασὶν ὅσοι ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσιν
ἡμέας ἀμφοτέρους, μάλα εἰκέλω ἀλλήλοιϊν
ἔμμεναι, ὡς σύ περ αὐτὴ ἐπιφρονέουσ’ ἀγορεύεις.
sentences.l:
“Old woman, thus they say, as many as saw with their eyes
us both, very like each other two
to be, as you yourself, thoughtfully, say.”
sentences.i: “Old woman, that is what they all say who have seen the two of us with their own eyes: that we are very like one another, just as you yourself say, thoughtfully.”
sentences.n: ὦ γρηῦ is 'old woman'. οὕτω φασίν … ἔμμεναι is 'so they say … to be', ἔμμεναι being the Homeric infinitive of εἰμί (Attic εἶναι); ὅσοι ἴδον is 'all who saw' (ἴδον is unaugmented). ἡμέας is ἡμᾶς 'us', ἀμφοτέρους 'both'; εἰκέλω and ἀλλήλοιϊν are dual forms, 'two alike', 'to one another'. ὡς σύ περ αὐτή is 'as you yourself'. ἐπιφρονέουσα is 'thinking carefully', from ἐπίφρων, the word of ἐπίφρονα in 326. He does not agree on his own account but reports what others say.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, γρηῢς δὲ λέβηθ’ ἕλε παμφανόωντα
τοῦ πόδας ἐξαπένιζεν, ὕδωρ δ’ ἐνεχεύατο πουλὺ
ψυχρόν, ἔπειτα δὲ θερμὸν ἐπήφυσεν.
sentences.l:
So then he spoke, and the old woman a cauldron took, all-shining,
his feet she began to wash off, and water she poured in, much,
cold, and then hot she added.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the old woman took an all-shining cauldron and began to wash his feet; she poured in a good deal of cold water, and then added hot.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη is 'so then he spoke', the speaker being Odysseus. λέβηθ’ is λέβητα with its last vowel lost and the τ aspirated before the rough breathing of ἕλε (unaugmented 'took'); λέβης is 'cauldron' by the house rendering, here the vessel she fills for the washing. παμφανόωντα is 'all-shining', stretched by diectasis. τοῦ is the pronoun 'his' (genitive of ὁ), and ἐξαπένιζεν is the imperfect 'began to wash off'. ἐνεχεύατο is the aorist middle of ἐγχέω 'pour in', and πουλύ is πολύ. ἐπήφυσεν is 'added by drawing', from ἐπαφύσσω.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἷζεν ἐπ’ ἐσχαρόφιν, ποτὶ δὲ σκότον ἐτράπετ’ αἶψα·
sentences.l:
But Odysseus
sat at the hearth, and toward the dark he turned at once;
sentences.i: But Odysseus sat at the hearth and at once turned himself toward the dark;
sentences.n: ἷζεν is the imperfect 'sat'. ἐσχαρόφιν has the suffix -φιν, which marks 'at, from' a place: ἐπ’ ἐσχαρόφιν is 'at the hearth'. ποτί is πρός, and σκότον is 'darkness'. ἐτράπετο is the aorist middle of τρέπω, 'turned himself'. The reason comes in the next two lines.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα γὰρ κατὰ θυμὸν ὀΐσατο, μή ἑ λαβοῦσα
οὐλὴν ἀμφράσσαιτο καὶ ἀμφαδὰ ἔργα γένοιτο.
sentences.l:
for at once in his heart he suspected, lest him taking hold of
the scar she should notice, and the deeds open would become.
sentences.i: for at once he suspected in his heart that she might take hold of him and notice the scar, and then the whole matter would be out in the open.
sentences.n: αὐτίκα γάρ is 'for at once'; κατὰ θυμόν is 'in his heart'. ὀΐσατο is the aorist of ὀΐομαι 'suspect'. μή here is 'lest': μή ἑ λαβοῦσα … ἀμφράσσαιτο is 'lest, taking hold of him, she notice', ἑ being the pronoun 'him', λαβοῦσα 'taking hold of', and ἀμφράσσαιτο the aorist optative of ἀμφράζομαι 'notice, observe'. οὐλήν is 'scar'. ἀμφαδά is 'open, plain', and ἔργα 'doings, the matter in hand'.

sentences.t: νίζε δ’ ἄρ’ ἆσσον ἰοῦσα ἄναχθ’ ἑόν·
sentences.l: And she then washed, nearer coming, her own lord;
sentences.i: She came nearer and began to wash her own lord;
sentences.n: νίζε is the imperfect of νίζω, 'was washing, began to wash'. ἆσσον is 'nearer'. ἄναχθ’ is ἄνακτα (ἄναξ 'lord') with its last vowel lost and the κ aspirated before the rough breathing of ἑόν. ἑόν is the possessive 'her own', the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν that is easily mistaken for the relative.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἔγνω
οὐλήν, τήν ποτέ μιν σῦς ἤλασε λευκῷ ὀδόντι
Παρνησόνδ’ ἐλθόντα μετ’ Αὐτόλυκόν τε καὶ υἷας,
sentences.l:
at once she knew
the scar, which once him a boar struck with a white tooth
to Parnassus going, to Autolycus and his sons,
sentences.i: At once she recognised the scar, which a boar had once struck him with its white tusk when he went to Parnassus, to Autolycus and his sons,
sentences.n: ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω, 'recognised'. οὐλήν is 'scar', and τήν ποτε μιν is 'which once … him': τήν is the relative, μιν 'him'. σῦς is 'boar' (σῦς = ὗς 'swine'; here a wild one), ἤλασε the aorist of ἐλαύνω 'drive, strike', and λευκῷ ὀδόντι 'with a white tooth', that is, a tusk. Παρνησόνδε has the suffix -δε of motion, 'to Parnassus'; ἐλθόντα agrees with μιν. μετ’ with the accusative is 'to join, in quest of'; υἷας is υἱεῖς 'sons', Autolycus's sons.

sentences.t:
μητρὸς ἑῆς πάτερ’ ἐσθλόν, ὃς ἀνθρώπους ἐκέκαστο
κλεπτοσύνῃ θ’ ὅρκῳ τε·
sentences.l:
of his own mother the father, good, who men had excelled
in thievery and in oath;
sentences.i: his own mother’s father, a good man, who excelled other men in thievery and in oath;
sentences.n: Autolycus, named in the last unit, is described: μητρὸς ἑῆς πάτερ’ ἐσθλόν is 'the good father of his own mother', ἑῆς being the possessive 'his own' (Odysseus's), and πάτερ’ being πατέρα with its last vowel lost. ἐσθλός is 'good'; the word praises skill, not honesty. ἐκέκαστο is a pluperfect of καίνυμαι 'excel', used as a simple past, with the accusative ἀνθρώπους 'men' and the datives κλεπτοσύνῃ 'in thievery' and ὅρκῳ 'in oath'. What skill in oaths amounts to, the line does not say.

sentences.t:
θεὸς δέ οἱ αὐτὸς ἔδωκεν
Ἑρμείας·
sentences.l:
and a god himself to him gave,
Hermes;
sentences.i: Hermes himself, a god, gave it to him;
sentences.n: θεός and Ἑρμείας are in apposition, 'a god … Hermes', the name held back to the start of the next line, with αὐτός 'himself'; Ἑρμείας is the epic form of Ἑρμῆς. οἱ is 'to him', Autolycus. ἔδωκεν has no object in the Greek: what was given is the skill just named.

sentences.t:
τῷ γὰρ κεχαρισμένα μηρία καῖεν
ἀρνῶν ἠδ’ ἐρίφων·
sentences.l:
for to him pleasing thigh-pieces he burned,
of lambs and of kids;
sentences.i: for he used to burn pleasing thigh-pieces for him, from lambs and kids;
sentences.n: τῷ is 'to him', Hermes, and the subject of καῖεν 'used to burn' is Autolycus. κεχαρισμένα is 'pleasing', the perfect passive participle of χαρίζομαι 'please'. μηρία are 'thigh-pieces' for the altar fire. ἀρνῶν and ἐρίφων are 'of lambs' and 'of kids' (ἀρήν 'lamb', ἔριφος 'kid').

sentences.t: ὁ δέ οἱ πρόφρων ἅμ’ ὀπήδει.
sentences.l: and he to him, ready-minded, together kept company.
sentences.i: and he, with a ready mind, kept him company.
sentences.n: ὁ is the pronoun 'he', Hermes, and οἱ is 'to him', Autolycus. πρόφρων is 'ready-minded', 'with a ready mind', as in the house rendering. ὀπήδει is the imperfect of ὀπηδέω 'accompany, keep company with', and ἅμ’ is ἅμα 'along'. The unit says how the gift of 396 came to be given: the god followed the man who sacrificed to him.

sentences.t:
Αὐτόλυκος δ’ ἐλθὼν Ἰθάκης ἐς πίονα δῆμον
παῖδα νέον γεγαῶτα κιχήσατο θυγατέρος ἧς·
sentences.l:
And Autolycus, having come to the rich land of Ithaca,
a child newly born found of his own daughter;
sentences.i: And Autolycus, coming to the rich land of Ithaca, found his own daughter’s child, newly born;
sentences.n: Ἰθάκης ἐς πίονα δῆμον is 'to the rich land of Ithaca': πίων is 'fat, rich', here 'rich', and δῆμος 'land'. παῖδα νέον γεγαῶτα is 'a child newly born' (a perfect participle of γίγνομαι); κιχήσατο is the aorist of κιχάνω 'come upon, find'. θυγατέρος ἧς is 'of his own daughter', ἧς being the possessive: Autolycus's daughter is Odysseus's mother, and the child is the infant Odysseus. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted, at its end: scanning it needs a lengthened syllable in θυγατέρος (fifth foot) and the old digamma of ἧς to make the syllable before it long (sixth foot).

sentences.t:
τόν ῥά οἱ Εὐρύκλεια φίλοις ἐπὶ γούνασι θῆκε
παυομένῳ δόρποιο, ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.l:
Him then for him Eurycleia upon dear knees set,
as he ceased from supper, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: Eurycleia set the child upon his knees just as he finished his supper, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: τόν is the pronoun 'him', the child; ῥά is ἄρα, and οἱ is 'for him', Autolycus. Εὐρύκλεια is the subject: the nurse of the household places the baby on his grandfather's knees (φίλοις 'dear', here 'his own'). παυομένῳ is the dative participle of παύω 'cease', agreeing with οἱ, and δόρποιο the genitive of what he leaves off, 'from supper'. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν is the formula 'and spoke a word and called him by name' (ἐκ … ὀνόμαζεν is a tmesis of ἐξονομάζω); the speaker is Eurycleia, and her words come after the end of this part.
